summary: Defines a new DNS resource record, GPOS, for recording geographical position, along with its type mnemonic and numeric code. It is an experimental protocol.

eli5.summary: A new entry for the internet's name book that says where on Earth a computer is.

questions: store latitude and longitude in dns
what is the dns gpos record
how to store location in dns
subtitle: A DNS record type for storing where on Earth a computer is located.

tldr.problem: It is hard to find the geographical location of an internet host. Administrators need to know where servers are situated for network management and troubleshooting.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1712 defines a new DNS resource record called GPOS (Geographical Position) that stores latitude, longitude, and altitude as text strings, with the DNS acting as a distributed database.
tldr.outcome: GPOS records can be queried alongside other DNS records, letting tools like traceroute be enhanced with geographical information. The RFC is Experimental.

today: RFC 1712 is Experimental and has not been adopted as a standard. While the idea is sound, GPOS never became widely deployed. Modern geolocation services typically use IP address databases rather than DNS records.

sections.title: The Problem of Locating Hosts
sections.content: The RFC begins with a practical problem: as the Internet grows, administrators and network tools need to know where physical servers are located. Existing tools like whois, traceroute, and nslookup could be vastly improved with geographical location information. The RFC frames location data as critical for network management—for instance, to identify which server is closest or to plan backbone connectivity.
sections.eli5: Network managers need to know where their computers are in the real world. Tools like traceroute could be much more useful if they could also show you what country or city a server is in.

sections.title: Why DNS Works Better Than Alternatives
sections.content: The RFC considers three alternatives. An SNMP approach would require all hosts to run a management agent with public read access—impractical. The X.500 Directory was too immature at the time. DNS, however, is already widely deployed, understood, and distributed. It delegates local administration (each domain administrator updates their own records) but makes data globally queryable. This matches the RFC's needs perfectly: information updated locally but available worldwide.
sections.eli5: The RFC looked at other ways to store location data but chose DNS because it's already everywhere, easy to update locally, and works globally.

sections.title: The GPOS Record Format
sections.content:
The GPOS record has four fields. The type code is 27, and the mnemonic is GPOS. The record contains three coordinate values: longitude (ranging from -180 to 180 degrees, positive east of the prime meridian), latitude (ranging from -90 to 90 degrees, positive north of the equator), and altitude (in meters above mean sea level). Each field is encoded as a printable text string rather than binary, allowing for arbitrary precision. The RFC gives an example: Curtin University in Perth, Western Australia is recorded as GPOS -32.6882 116.8652 10.0.

Text strings avoid floating-point precision loss and allow administrators to record measurements with whatever precision they have available. Each field is limited to 256 characters, though the RFC recommends using the minimum necessary characters.
sections.eli5: A GPOS record is three numbers: how far east or west (longitude), how far north or south (latitude), and how high up in meters. They are written as text, not numbers, so you can be very precise.

sections.title: Using GPOS Records
sections.content:
Each host that wants to publish its location gets one GPOS field in its DNS zone file. If a host omits GPOS, DNS queries for that host simply return no location information. The RFC shows a real zone file excerpt where some hosts (marsh, lillee, ambrose) share the same location, while hinault is 10 degrees north in the mountains. The host merckx has no GPOS record, hiding its location for security reasons.

Most DNS server implementations at the time would ignore GPOS as an unknown record type and issue a warning—but they would accept the zone file and serve the record correctly when queried, allowing the protocol to be deployed without waiting for universal software support.
sections.eli5: Each computer's DNS entry can have a GPOS record. Some computers might not have one if the owner doesn't want to reveal where they are. Old DNS servers don't understand GPOS but still work fine.

sections.title: Public Information
sections.content: The RFC notes that once information enters the DNS, it is considered public. Publishing geographical coordinates reveals the physical location of infrastructure, which could be sensitive for security reasons. This is why administrators may choose to omit GPOS records for certain hosts, as the merckx example demonstrates.
sections.eli5: Once you put location information in DNS, everyone on the Internet can find it. That's why some computers don't have GPOS records—the owner wants to keep their location secret.

fields.name: Longitude
fields.desc: Text string, -180.0 to 180.0, positive east of prime meridian.

fields.name: Latitude
fields.desc: Text string, -90.0 to 90.0, positive north of equator.

fields.name: Altitude
fields.desc: Text string in meters above mean sea level.
